Worldly Sorrow
WURLD-lee SOR-oh
doctrinal phrase
From worldly (of this present age) and sorrow (grief); the false grief Paul contrasts with godly sorrow.

📖 Biblical Definition

Worldly sorrow is the false and fruitless grief over sin that springs not from love to God but from love to self—the regret of one sorry for the consequences of his sin rather than for the sin itself, which Paul says “worketh death.” The apostle draws the sharp contrast: “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” Godly sorrow grieves that God has been offended, hates the sin as sin, and turns the soul to God in genuine repentance that issues in changed life; it produces, as Paul lists, carefulness, indignation against the sin, fear, vehement desire, zeal, and the setting right of wrong. Worldly sorrow, by contrast, mourns only the loss, the shame, the punishment, or the exposure—it weeps over the wages of sin while still loving the sin; it is the remorse of Cain, who feared his punishment, and of Judas, who was filled with remorse and went and hanged himself, but never repented unto life; whereas Peter, with godly sorrow, wept bitterly and was restored. The dictionary holds the distinction as vital to discerning true conversion: many sorrow for sin who are never saved, for their grief is self-centered and barren. Worldly sorrow may look like repentance and even shed many tears, yet it works death; only godly sorrow, grieving that God is dishonored and turning to Him through Christ, works repentance unto salvation.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The false, self-centered grief over sin’s consequences—not over the sin itself—which Paul says worketh death, contrasted with godly sorrow that worketh repentance unto salvation.

WORLDLY SORROW, false grief over sin springing from love of self, not love of God.

“The sorrow of the world worketh death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Mourns the consequences, shame, or punishment while still loving the sin.

The remorse of Cain and of Judas, who never repented unto life.

Contrasted with godly sorrow, which worketh repentance to salvation.

📖 Key Scripture

2Co 7:10 — "For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."

Mat 27:3 — "Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,"

Luk 22:62 — "And Peter went out, and wept bitterly."

2Co 7:11 — "For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Mere regret over consequences is mistaken for true repentance, and the distinguishing of false from godly sorrow is lost.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul’s sharp distinction between two sorrows that may look alike but lead to opposite ends. Worldly sorrow weeps over the wages of sin—the exposure, the shame, the punishment—while the heart still loves the sin; godly sorrow grieves that God has been offended and turns the soul from sin to God. The one worketh death; the other, repentance unto salvation. A therapy-culture that treats all grief over wrongdoing as equally healing cannot make this distinction; Scripture insists upon it.

The contrast of Judas and Peter makes it plain. Both grieved bitterly over their sin against Christ; but Judas’s sorrow was the despairing remorse of the world, which drove him to the rope, while Peter’s was godly sorrow that wept and returned and was restored. The dictionary holds the difference as a vital test of conversion: many tears are shed in worldly sorrow that never reach repentance. Only the grief that hates sin as against God, and flees to Christ for pardon, works the repentance that is unto life.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the false grief over sin’s consequences that works death, set against the godly sorrow that works repentance.

expand to see more

Greek lupē — sorrow, grief; the word for both sorrows in 2 Corinthians 7.

“Of the world,” tou kosmou — springing from this present age and the love of self.

Greek metanoia — repentance, the change of mind godly sorrow works.

Judas’s remorse (metamelomai) is distinguished from saving repentance.

Peter’s bitter weeping is the pattern of godly sorrow restored.

Usage

"Worldly sorrow is preached as the counterfeit of true repentance."

"Judas and Peter are contrasted to distinguish the two sorrows."

"It warns that tears over sin’s consequences are not yet repentance unto life."
